title: How to Woodenize Working Memory (Woodenization Example)
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. presents a classroom-ready "Woodenization" mini-lesson — his term for explicitly teaching a concept students need but rarely receive direct instruction in — built around the limits of working memory. He explains working memory as the small, universally limited set of "chunks" anyone can hold in mind at once, demonstrating the limit to students through a number-memorization exercise before introducing two vivid metaphors for overload: an iceberg island that can only hold so many penguins, and Barbara Oakley's metaphor of choking on too much food. From Oakley's book Learn Like a Pro, he draws three concrete strategies for managing working-memory limits — simplifying information into one's own words, deliberately ignoring complicating details at first, and writing things down — summarized in his own recurring classroom line, "Paper is cheap, but learning is priceless." He frames the whole exercise as quick to deliver but disproportionately valuable, tying it directly to the Effort, Efficacy, Credibility, and Belonging beliefs from his Five Key Beliefs motivation framework.
points: Stuart uses a concrete classroom demonstration — having students memorize number lists and count how many they retain — to make the abstract limit on working memory tangible before teaching around it.

He offers students two competing metaphors for cognitive overload (an iceberg island of penguins; choking on too much food, borrowed from Barbara Oakley) to give multiple mental handles on the same concept.

Drawing on Oakley's Learn Like a Pro, he distills three actionable strategies for managing working-memory limits: simplify into your own words, ignore complicating detail at first, and write things down.
His recurring classroom line — "Paper is cheap, but learning is priceless" — functions as a compressed, repeatable argument for note-taking that survives despite student eye-rolls.
He explicitly ties this brief mini-lesson to four of his Five Key Beliefs (Effort, Efficacy, Credibility, Belonging), arguing quick cognitive-science explainers carry outsized motivational payoff.
quotes: The trouble with working memory, I tell my students, is that it is limited. For everyone. No matter how smart you are, you've got less than a handful of chunks in working memory.
Picture your working memory as a small iceberg island, and each thing you're thinking about is a penguin. The island can only hold so many penguins. Add too many, and a penguin has to slip off.
It feels bad to overload your working memory, just like it feels bad to choke on too much food. This "choking" language is what Barbara Oakley uses in her bestselling A Mind for Numbers.
Systems of writing are THE greatest mind-expanding invention ever made by human beings. Whenever my students CAN take notes to keep penguins on the island, I tell them they SHOULD take notes.
This kind of work is pretty quick in the classroom, but what it's doing for the Effort and Efficacy (not to mention Credibility and Belonging) beliefs is not to be scoffed at.
